label: Western Desert Painting
defn: The acrylic painting movement of the Central and Western Desert begun at Papunya in 1971, in which Dreaming (Tjukurrpa/Jukurrpa) designs once made in sand, body paint and ceremony are painted on canvas and board in dotted and concentric-circle fields, carried on by community art centres: Papunya Tula boards, Warlukurlangu Jukurrpa canvases, Utopia and APY Lands painting.
aliases: Western Desert art movement;dot painting;Papunya Tula painting;acrylic desert painting
note: Western Desert art movement and Dot painting both redirect to Papunya Tula; art centres are kinds; Utopia (Anmatyerre/Alyawarr, Arandic) is placed here by convention as Central Desert painting

label: Contemporary Indigenous Australian Art
defn: Painting by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander artists from the 1970s onward outside the Western Desert and bark-painting lineages, in ochre and acrylic on canvas, worked through community art centres: Warmun (Turkey Creek) ochre paintings, Mangkaja and Ngukurr acrylics, Mornington Island painting, Mowanjum Wandjina paintings.
note: kept narrow in use: holds the painting centres that have no leaf of their own; the article title is the movement umbrella (see problems)

label: Hermannsburg School
defn: The Western Arrernte watercolour landscape school of the Hermannsburg mission (from 1934), founded by Albert Namatjira after lessons with Rex Battarbee and carried on by his family and followers: MacDonnell Ranges landscapes, ghost gums.
note: artists (Namatjira, Pannka) are artist-led

label: Bark Painting
defn: Painting in natural ochres on prepared stringybark sheets, the classic medium of Arnhem Land, with clan designs in fine cross-hatching (rarrk) in the east and figurative and x-ray figures in the west: Yolŋu miny'tji clan paintings, Kunwinjku x-ray figures, Groote Eylandt black-ground barks.
note: art centres and regional schools are kinds; Tiwi painted bark baskets (tunga) see L18

label: Torres Strait Islander Printmaking
defn: The linocut and etching movement of the Torres Strait (Zenadth Kes) from the 1990s, cutting island cosmology, totems and turtle-shell mask forms into large black-and-white prints: Badu and Moa linocuts, Mabuiag etchings.
note: printmakers (Tipoti, Nona, Bosun, Missi) are artist-led

label: Torres Strait Turtle-Shell Masks
defn: Masks of the Torres Strait Islands built from heated and stitched turtle-shell plates, worn in initiation, funerary and increase ceremonies, with composite human-animal forms in the west and human faces in the east: krar (western islands), le op (Mer, Erub), crocodile-head masks.
note: dhari (feather headdress) and wooden mawa masks of Saibai are kinds

label: Whakairo
defn: Māori wood carving: the carved figures, panels, gateways and canoe prows of meeting houses (wharenui), storehouses and canoes, cut in regional and tribal schools with manaia, spiral and figure motifs: poupou wall panels, pātaka storehouse carvings, tauihu canoe prows, waka huia treasure boxes.
note: iwi schools and named carvers are kinds; the meeting house as a building is K12

label: Malagan
defn: The carved and painted funerary sculpture of northern New Ireland, made for malagan memorial ceremonies and discarded after display: openwork friezes, figures and masks of softwood with opercula eyes: vavara friezes, totok poles, tatanua masks.

label: Uli
defn: The massive hermaphroditic ancestor figures of central New Ireland (Mandak and Barak), displayed in the long ceremonies of skull reburial: uli figures with raised arms and crested headdresses.

label: Asmat Woodcarving
defn: The wood carving of the Asmat of south-west New Guinea (Papua, Indonesia), carvers (wowipits) working in the tradition of the culture hero Fumeripits: bisj ancestor poles, carved shields, canoe prows, ancestor figures.

label: Sepik Carving
defn: The figure sculpture, masks and ceremonial-house carving of the peoples of the Sepik River basin of Papua New Guinea: Iatmul orator's stools and ancestor figures, Sawos malu boards, Abelam yam masks and ancestor figures.
note: Abelam sago-spathe ceiling painting and Sawos/Aibom pottery are not under this leaf (see problems)

label: Massim Carving
defn: The curvilinear carving of the Massim region (Milne Bay, PNG), above all the Trobriand Islands, in hardwood incised and filled with lime: tabuya and lagim canoe prow boards for kula voyages, lime spatulas, dance shields.

label: Nguzu Nguzu
defn: The blackened wood canoe-prow figureheads of New Georgia in the western Solomon Islands, inlaid with nautilus shell, the emblem of the Solomon Islands shell-inlay tradition: nguzu nguzu figureheads, shell-inlaid bowls.
note: label is the field's object name; it stands for the shell-inlay carving of New Georgia (see problems)

label: Marquesan Carving
defn: The carving of the Marquesas Islands (Te Henua ʻEnana) in wood, bone and stone, dense with the eye-and-face (mata) motifs shared with Marquesan tattoo: uʻu clubs, tiki figures, carved bowls and fan handles, bone ear ornaments (taiana).

label: Moai Kavakava
defn: The small wooden figures of Rapa Nui (Easter Island) carved in toromiro, emaciated male ancestor images worn at feasts, with their companion carvings: moai kavakava, moai paepae, rei miro pectorals.
note: label is an object type standing for Rapa Nui wood carving (see problems); stone moai are K/D monumental

label: Aurukun Sculpture
defn: The ochre-painted softwood sculpture of the Wik and Kugu peoples of Aurukun on Cape York, made for ceremony and since the 1990s through the art centre: Ku' (camp dog) figures, ancestral beings.

label: Hei-tiki
defn: Māori ornaments carved from pounamu (New Zealand nephrite and bowenite) with stone tools, worn as heirlooms (taonga): hei-tiki human figure pendants, hei matau hook pendants, kuru ear pendants, mere pounamu clubs.
note: label per the field; the leaf covers pounamu ornament carving

label: Pukumani Poles
defn: The carved and ochre-painted ironwood grave posts (tutini) of the Tiwi Islands, erected round the grave at the Pukumani mourning ceremony and crowned with painted bark baskets: tutini, tunga bark baskets, carved figures.
note: Tiwi ochre painting on canvas sits under L2 as a kind

label: Toas
defn: Small painted direction-markers of gypsum, wood and found materials made by the Diyari and neighbouring peoples of the Lake Eyre basin about 1904, left to show where a group had gone.

label: Riji
defn: Pearl-shell pendants and pubic coverings of the Kimberley, engraved with interlocking meanders and filled with ochre, worn in ceremony and traded far inland: riji, jakoli, longkalongka.
note: shell ornament filed in G3 for want of a non-metal ornament sub-family (see problems)

label: Māori Weaving
defn: The fibre arts of the Māori in harakeke (New Zealand flax) and muka (its fibre): finger-twined (whatu) cloaks with tāniko borders and plaited (raranga) baskets and mats: kaitaka and korowai cloaks, piupiu, kete, whāriki.
note: plaited raranga (kete, whāriki) sits under this leaf, not H8, to keep the culture's weaving in one place

label: Tivaevae
defn: The appliqué and piecework quilts of the Cook Islands (and tīfaifai of Tahiti), sewn communally by women's groups (vainetini) and given at weddings, birthdays and funerals: tivaevae manu, tivaevae taorei, tivaevae tataura.

label: Possum-Skin Cloak
defn: Cloaks of sewn possum pelts incised on the skin side with clan and Country designs, worn by the Aboriginal peoples of south-eastern Australia and revived since the 1990s: Lake Condah and Maiden's Punt cloaks, revival cloaks.
note: SE Australian carved shields and clubs in the same row have no leaf (see problems)

label: Tapa Cloth
defn: Barkcloth beaten from paper-mulberry and other inner bark across the Pacific and painted, stencilled, rubbed or printed with designs: Samoan siapo, Tongan ngatu, Fijian masi, Hawaiian kapa, Niuean hiapo, Omie and Maisin barkcloth.
note: island traditions are kinds

label: ʻIe Tōga
defn: The finely plaited pandanus fine mats of Samoa, and the fine mats of Tonga and Tuvalu, exchanged as the highest valuables at life-crisis ceremonies: ʻie tōga, Tongan kie and taʻovala.

label: Aboriginal Fibre Art
defn: The coiled, looped, twined and plaited fibre work of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women and men, from string bags and baskets to contemporary fibre sculpture: dillybags, Arnhem Land pandanus baskets, rainforest bicornual baskets, Tjanpi grass sculpture, ghost-net sculpture.

label: Lalava
defn: Decorative coconut-fibre (sennit, magimagi) lashing of Tonga, Fiji and Samoa, binding the beams of houses and the hulls of canoes in red and black geometric patterns, now also made as freestanding works.

label: Hawaiian Featherwork
defn: The featherwork of the Hawaiian chiefs: red and yellow honeyeater and ʻiʻiwi feathers knotted to olonā netting as emblems of rank and divinity: ʻahu ʻula cloaks and capes, mahiole helmets, lei hulu, feathered god images.

label: Kahu Huruhuru
defn: Māori feather cloaks: muka cloaks finger-woven (whatu) with feathers of kiwi, kererū, kākā and other birds set in the weft, the highest-ranking cloaks of the 19th century onward: kahu kiwi, kahu kererū.
note: attest by the redirect Kahu huruhuru to its section

label: Fijian Clubs
defn: The carved hardwood war clubs (i-wau) of Fiji, made by specialist carvers in named forms and often finely incised: totokia (pineapple club), gata (gunstock club), i-ula throwing clubs, kinikini paddle clubs.
note: Tongan clubs (ʻakau tau) are a see-also gap

label: Vanuatu Slit Gongs
defn: The upright slit gongs of northern Vanuatu (Ambrym, Malakula), breadfruit trunks hollowed and carved with ancestral faces and raised in dancing grounds of the grade societies: atingting kon (Ambrym), Malakula slit gongs; tree-fern grade figures as a kind.

label: Hermannsburg Potters
defn: The hand-built, painted terracotta of the Western Arrernte women of Hermannsburg (Ntaria) since 1990, with modelled animal lids and landscapes painted in underglaze: lidded pots.
note: an art-centre ware

label: Arnhem Land Rock Art
defn: The painted rock shelters of the western Arnhem Land plateau and Kakadu, from Dynamic figures to the recent x-ray and contact paintings: Ubirr, Burrungkuy (Nourlangie), Nanguluwur, Injalak Hill.

label: Gwion Gwion Rock Paintings
defn: The fine-line figure paintings of the north-west Kimberley, slender tasselled human figures of great age.
note: Wandjina rock paintings of the same region are a kind (see problems)

label: Murujuga Rock Art
defn: The petroglyphs of the Burrup Peninsula and Dampier Archipelago (Murujuga), over a million engravings made across tens of thousands of years.

label: Sydney Rock Engravings
defn: The outline engravings on Hawkesbury sandstone in the Sydney basin: animals, ancestral beings and people: Ku-ring-gai Chase sites.

label: Quinkan Rock Art
defn: The painted shelters around Laura on Cape York with the Quinkan spirit figures.

label: Panaramitee Style
defn: The widespread Australian engraving style of tracks, circles and dots ('track and circle'), among the oldest rock art of the continent: Ewaninga, Panaramitee.

label: Māori Rock Art
defn: The charcoal and red-ochre drawings in limestone shelters of South Canterbury and North Otago: Takiroa, Awamoko.
note: Māori rock art redirects to Māori culture#Painting

label: Tā Moko
defn: Māori tattooing, chiselled (uhi) into the skin in curvilinear designs that mark descent and rank: moko on men's faces, moko kauae for women.

label: Polynesian Tattooing
defn: The tattoo traditions of Polynesia worked with toothed combs and a mallet: Samoan peʻa and malu, Marquesan full-body tattoo, Tahitian tatau, Fijian veiqia.
note: Peʻa attests the Samoan core; Polynesian tattoo redirects to History of tattooing#Polynesia
